newsitem.title: JAPAN: US seen delaying Japan port sanction announcement.
newsitem.headline: US seen delaying Japan port sanction announcement.

text.p: The United States appears to have made up its mind whether to slap sanctions on Japanese shipping firms over Japan's port practices but has delayed an announcement of the decision, a U.S. official said on Friday.

Japanese media suggested that Washington wanted to delay announcing a decision to impose sanctions on three shipping companies to avoid upsetting U.S.-Japan ties ahead of Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's visit to Japan.
Albright is set to arrive in Tokyo on Sunday for talks with Japanese leaders as part of a globe-circling trip, her first since taking office last month.

"The FMC (Federal Maritime Commission) met on February 19 as scheduled and they appear to have made a decision on how to proceed," a U.S. embassy official told Reuters. "But they are going to be holding off on an announcement until some unspecified date in the near future."

The FMC, angry at what it says are discriminatory and costly Japanese port practices, has been considering slapping a $100,000 surcharge on ship operators Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd, Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd and Nippon Yusen KK every time they stop at a U.S. port.

The FMC charged that Japan's Transport Ministry discourages applications for cargo handling licences and that the need to consult the Japan Harbour and Transport Authority (JHTA) for changes in all vessel operations, no matter how minor, gives the JHTA effective control over port business in Japan.
The European Union has also complained about the Japanese port practices.

The Japanese shipping companies, however, argue that the FMC charges are not based on facts and that they do not decide port practices. Earlier this month, they petitioned the independent U.S. regulatory body to drop the sanction plan.

Some trade experts have speculated that the FMC might decide to impose sanctions but to delay the starting date for the sanctions by days, weeks or even months. That would allow talks to continue, but under greater U.S. pressure.

High-profile U.S.-Japan trade disputes have often gone to the brink and but averted the actual imposition of sanctions by last-minute deals. That was the case in a bitter feud over trade in cars and car parts in 1995. Two-way trade spats have been on the back-burner recently, but analysts say tempers could flare later this year if Tokyo's trade surplus with Washington rises again due to the weak yen.

On Friday Japan's trade ministry dismissed as "groundless" U.S. allegations, filed with a World Trade Organisation dispute settlement panel, that the Japanese government had attempted to thwart foreign entry into its photographic film and paper market.
